title: CNN
body:
A [[Neural Network]] that **drops the fully-connected assumption** and replaces it with two
constraints borrowed from the structure of images. Everything else (the [[Loss Function]],
[[Back Propagation]], [[Gradient Descent]]) is unchanged; only the shape of the
[[Weights]] differs.

## The two ideas

A [[Multilayer Perceptron]] flattens a $28 \times 28$ image into a 784-entry [[Vector]], which
throws away the single most useful fact about it: **pixel 5 and pixel 6 are neighbours and pixel 5
and pixel 500 are not.** The network then has to relearn that from data, at enormous cost in
[[Weights]]. A CNN builds it in instead:

- **Local connectivity.** A unit looks at a small patch (3×3, 5×5), not the whole image. Whatever
  detects an edge only needs to see the pixels around that edge.
- **Weight sharing.** The *same* patch of weights, called a filter or kernel, slides across the
  whole image. An edge detector is an edge detector wherever it is applied, so there is no reason
  to learn a separate one per position.

Weight sharing is what makes the parameter count collapse. A fully connected layer on
$28 \times 28$ input with 100 units is 78,400 weights; a convolutional layer with 32 filters of
$3\times3$ is $32 \times 9 = 288$, regardless of image size. It also buys **translation
equivariance** for free: shift the input and the feature map shifts with it, so a digit is
recognised the same in either corner without ever being shown it there.

## The operation

Convolution here is: slide the filter over the input, take a [[Dot Product]] at every position,
write the result into a feature map. It is [[Matrix Multiplication]] with a constrained, heavily
repeated matrix, so [[Forward Pass]] still describes what happens. Each of the $k$ filters produces
its own feature map, and depth in the channel direction is how a layer holds several different
detectors at once.

Pooling (usually max over a $2\times2$ window) then downsamples, which shrinks the maps, widens
what a later unit effectively sees, and makes the representation tolerant of small shifts. A
typical stack is `conv → [[ReLU]] → pool`, repeated, then a couple of fully connected layers and a
softmax [[Output Layer]].

The feature hierarchy this produces is the one case in [[MACHINE LEARNING]] where the story is
actually visible: early filters learn oriented edges, middle layers learn textures and corners,
late layers learn object parts. See [[Hidden Layer]].

## Where it applies

Anything with a grid and a locality assumption. [[Computer Vision]] above all, which is what it was
built for, and [[MNIST]] is the standard demonstration: a CNN gets past 99% where a flat
[[Multilayer Perceptron]] stalls lower with far more parameters. Audio spectrograms and time series
use the 1-D version. Note the assumption is a real one, and it fails: on tabular data where column
order is arbitrary there is no locality to exploit and a CNN buys nothing.

The classical predecessor is worth knowing, because [[Principal Component Analysis]] on face images
(eigenfaces) is the linear version of the same ambition: find a small set of components that
explain images. A CNN learns non-linear, local, shared ones instead. See
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] and [[Image Processing]].
